scope: Scene-local Kokoro word boundaries and measured audio durations. The opening and exact-metric scenes use the revised script. All unchanged takes retain their original measurements.

changed.previousSay: Here's the first report from our Python scorer. Here's the second. Both look perfect. Yesterday we saved three requests. Pick the middle one, request one hundred two. Can you tell from these numbers whether either run scored it?

Open yesterday's file at that request. Here's the expected label. Beside it is the saved prediction. See the spaces just inside the quotes? The scorer trims spaces from both ends of each label and compares the words in lowercase. Should this row count as correct?

Yesterday's file set our baseline. Across the top are the expected labels. Underneath are the model's predictions after normalization. The two correct answers just clear the integer gate. Both sides are six. Leave the three request IDs where they are and bring back the reports from the opening.

Start each run from yesterday's file. In A a new prediction came back for the middle request. This time the model said blocked. Now all three match. In B, keep every prediction exactly as it was. Make one edit to the file. Remove request one hundred two. Look at the empty position. Both remaining predictions match their expected labels, so B scores two out of two. Now cover the counts again. Both reports look perfect, and both clear the floor. Which one contains evidence that the model got the hard case right?

beats.say: Two of these three predictions match. Take out the middle row. Both matches are still there, and now Python gives them a perfect score.

Put that row back. The expected label is blocked. The model saved escalated, with capitals and a space at each end. Python trims both labels and compares them in lowercase. Will it record True or False for this row?

Let's run that function on a copy of the Docker lab file. In the lab, request one hundred two says escalated in lowercase. Our copy uses capitals and a space at each end. Start in the project directory. The project file declares which Python versions the scorer supports. The checkout pin selects Python three twelve. Run uv sync to create the environment and, on this first setup, write the dependency lock.

Use uv run to launch the scorer in that environment. Path builds a path relative to the project directory we're standing in. Open the file as UTF eight and the loop visits one line at a time. The handle gives Python text. Each nonblank line here contains one JSON object.

The file gives us a line of text. The call to json dot loads decodes it into a Python dictionary. The equals sign binds that object to row. A dictionary lets you look up a value by name. The brackets around prediction take us straight to the saved label.

Keep an eye on the saved field while we normalize its value under a new name. Strip removes the spaces at its two ends. Lower then changes the capitals to lowercase. These methods return strings. The capitals are still there in the dictionary. We apply both methods to the expected label too.

Read the two words Python has after stripping and lowercasing. In this expression the double equals sign compares two values. The single equals sign gives the answer a name. The Boolean is False. That adds zero to the number of matches. How many places should this request take in the list of results?

Here's the loop. On each visit, row refers to one dictionary. Python runs the indented lines for that row before moving on. The first pair matches, so append True. Request one hundred two differs, so append False. The final pair matches, so append True. Look where the middle result landed.

Adding those Booleans counts each True as one and False as zero, giving two matches. Len counts all three Booleans. The middle request takes up a place just like its neighbors. Divide the counts to get two thirds. Python prints the fraction to three decimal places. We'll need the two integers again.

Start a fresh row with the two normalized labels from request one hundred two. The expected label is blocked and the prediction is escalated. Give the baseline list a second name, trial. Follow both arrows before you edit. Now set the trial prediction to blocked. Read it back through baseline. Both names lead to the dictionary you just changed.

Reset to escalated and copy the outer list. You can see two lists now. Follow slot zero in either one. Run the same mutation through trial. Both arrows still end at the same dictionary, so baseline reads blocked again.

Reset again. This comprehension copies each row into a new list. Now mutate the copied row. This time the baseline keeps escalated. Every value in this row is a string. What if one field held a list we could append to?

Let's give those two string operations a home. In exact match, the parameters name the expected label and the prediction. The indented body normalizes both. Return sends the comparison back to the loop. For blocked and escalated the return value is False.

Try a different caller. It supplies approved and a prediction in capitals with spaces around it. The function returns True after normalization. The string and Boolean hints tell a reader or a static checker what values the function expects and returns. What would happen if the caller passed seven?

Watch the integer enter the function. Python accepts the call. When Python looks up strip on seven, it can't find that method. It raises AttributeError before the method call. This function only received two values. To tell someone which line to fix, check the field while reading the file.

Yesterday's row made it all the way to a comparison. In a copy of the file, replace the prediction with a bare seven. Look at the quotes on the line above. Seven is legal JSON too. Decoding produces a dictionary with an integer value. Will that seven ever reach the comparison?

Now look at the field check. Each of the three required fields must be a string with at least one character left after stripping whitespace. Python found the field. Its value is an integer, so the type check tells Python to raise TypeError. The message gives us line two and the name prediction. There’s no Boolean for this row because the loader stopped here.

Keep the rest of the line and erase the seven. The closing brace comes immediately after the colon. This time the line fails inside json dot loads. The loader adds line two to that error. Look across the three versions. The original gives the scorer two text labels to compare. The middle line tells us someone saved a seven. On the last line, decoding stopped before we even had a field to check.

Here's our three-row file again. Each column holds one request, with its expected label above its prediction. Two matches out of three put us exactly on the floor. Both sides are six. How else could this file earn a perfect score?

Run A gets a new prediction for the middle request. This time the model said blocked. Now all three match. Start B from the original rows. Keep the predictions. Remove request one hundred two. B scores two out of two. Now cover the counts. Both runs clear the floor. Which one got the middle request right?

Read down the column for request one hundred two. Only A has a new answer for that request. The scorer and the dependency lock are identical in both runs. Load file B in the test and check its exact counts against yesterday's fixture. The assertion fails. The match count held steady while the total fell. Open the input diff. That minus sign identifies the request B dropped. Restore the line before you compare models on this fixture.
